_comment: TWO gzip ceilings, in BYTES, and this file is the single source of truth for
both: `eagerChunkGzipMaxBytes` bounds the EAGER GRAPH as a total, and
`lazyChunkGzipMaxBytes` (#372) bounds EVERY OTHER emitted .js chunk
INDIVIDUALLY. (This line said 'The EAGER GRAPH's gzip ceiling' until #372
added the second key; correcting it here rather than leaving it standing is
this file's own rule.) It used to be prose in a docs/BACKLOG.md row, raised
and recorded by the same person, with no mechanical check in either
direction. It was raised twice in two PRs before anyone could notice.
MEASURE THE SHIPPING BUILD. The bundle must be built with VITE_API_LIVE=true
(what infra/docker/Dockerfile.api sets). A build without it is ~860 B LARGER
and is not what ships -- that discrepancy already made one reviewer report a
wrong figure. scripts/check-bundle-size.mjs builds that variant itself rather
than trusting whatever happens to be in dist/. (It does not 'assert the mode'
-- an earlier version tried to detect the mode from the built output and
silently never fired, because Vite constant-folds VITE_API_LIVE away.)
WHAT IS COUNTED (#323): the eager module graph as declared by VITE'S OWN BUILD
MANIFEST (dist/.vite/manifest.json) -- the entry chunk plus the transitive
closure of its static `imports`. `dynamicImports` are excluded, which is the
STATIC/DYNAMIC split -- NOT, as this line used to claim, exactly the
eager/lazy one. See the blind-spot list below, which measures the
difference rather than asserting it. (bundle-budget.mjs was corrected and
this copy was not -- the same file that calls itself the single source of
truth then contradicted itself six lines apart.)
Two earlier forms of this measurement were both wrong, in the same direction:
1. 'the largest dist/assets/index-*.js'. With manualChunks configured it
measured 19,594 B against a real eager graph of 65,284 B -- a 45,690 B
under-report, reporting headroom that did not exist.
2. 'the entry <script type=module> plus every <link rel=modulepreload> in
dist/index.html'. Correct for form 1's case, but with
build.modulePreload:false Vite emits NO preload links, so a statically
imported 45.69 kB vendor chunk vanished again. Preload links are a HINT;
the manifest is the build's own statement of the graph.
NOT counted BY THE EAGER KEY. The first is deliberate; the last two are
BLIND SPOTS, listed because an adversarial review LANDED both and because a
list that reads as exhaustive when it is not is worse than no list at all:
- CSS. A separate 9,169 B gzip (measured) that no version of either gate
has counted.
- Lazily-imported chunks. This line used to read 'which is the whole point
of the split' and stop there; #372 falsified it. They are now counted
INDIVIDUALLY against lazyChunkGzipMaxBytes. What remains uncounted is
their SUM (13,117 B today) and their COUNT (8 today) -- both RECORDED by
`npm run check:bundle` on every run and bounded by nothing.
- BLIND SPOT: anything in frontend/public/ pulled in by a plain
<script src> in index.html. Reproduced in review: a 73,869 B gzip
render-blocking script made the real eager JS 2.06x this ceiling while
the gate reported 1,678 B of headroom and the whole unit suite stayed
green. There is exactly ONE <script> in index.html today (the module
entry) and src/test/buildGuards.test.ts now pins that, which closes the
demonstrated path without teaching this gate to parse HTML.
- BLIND SPOT: an UNCONDITIONAL module-scope `import()`. Vite files it
under dynamicImports, so it is excluded from the EAGER number, yet the
browser fetches it on every load. Reproduced: an 80,020 B gzip chunk
moved the eager number by 2 B. So `dynamicImports` is the STATIC/DYNAMIC
split, not the eager/lazy one -- they coincide only while every dynamic
import sits behind a user action or a scroll, as all FIVE of this app's
do today (four clicks; landing-strip on scroll).
#372 made this blind spot WORSE, not better, and it is stated plainly:
such a chunk is filed under dynamicImports, so the new key classifies it
as 'lazy' and grants it a 6,328 B per-chunk allowance while the browser
fetches it on EVERY load. It went from UNCOUNTED to SANCTIONED.
One more thing the measurement is honest about: Fly passes a PRODUCTION
VITE_API_DEMO_KEY while this builds with the default, so the deployed bundle
differs by that key's length delta (sub-100 B). Dockerfile parity was
otherwise VERIFIED in review -- building the way infra/docker/Dockerfile.api
does emitted the SAME content hash as buildCommand().
BOTH KEY NAMES BELOW ARE LOAD-BEARING (this said 'The KEY NAME', singular,
until #372). Mistyping or renaming one used to make the gate read
`undefined`, compare `gz > undefined` (false), and print 'bundle budget OK
... headroom NaN B' for a bundle of any size, exit 0. Both now go through the
SAME validated `parseBudget(text, key)` path -- a positive integer or a hard
failure -- and the lazy comparison is additionally written in the positive
form `!(gzip <= max)` so that an `undefined` ceiling makes EVERY chunk a
violator instead of producing an empty violator list that passes.
WHY 68,000, AND WHAT IT IS PROTECTING AGAINST (set 2026-09-06)
The previous number, 66,000, was not chosen -- it was the last raise. Against
a graph measuring 65,931 B it left 69 B, i.e. 0.10%, so EVERY frontend change
of any size had become a budget negotiation. That is not a strict budget; it
is a budget that has stopped measuring growth and started blocking work. The
observed cost was not hypothetical: PR #357 CUT an accessibility announcement
-- a toast telling the reader their clicked question had been silently dropped
-- because it measured +62 B and there were 69 B left. A ceiling that makes
WCAG work the thing you trade away is measuring the wrong quantity.
WHAT THE GRAPH ACTUALLY IS, measured, not assumed. It is ONE file: vite.config
.ts declares no `build` block, so there is no manualChunks and the entry has
no static `imports` at all. Attributed by decoding the build's own sourcemap:
react-dom  130,102 B raw / ~41.9 kB gzip. That was 63.6% of the raw
PRE-CHANGE graph (#358-era, kept labelled because the
68,000 decision was argued from it). Against the graph that
SHIPS TODAY -- 193,208 B raw, measured -- the same 130,102 B is
67.3%. Corrected HERE, in place, rather than 130 lines further
down: this file's own rule, which it had broken by doing both
at once. The share drifts whenever app code does, so read it as
~two thirds, not as a pinned figure. The point gets STRONGER,
not weaker: app code shrank, so React is a larger share of what
is left, and no app-code change moves the dominant term.
react + scheduler + jsx-runtime      ~11.2 kB raw
ALL application code                  59,276 B raw / ~19 kB gzip
So roughly two thirds of this ceiling is React itself and cannot be moved by
any app-code change. Nobody should spend a week shaving components again.
WHY NOT SIMPLY TRIM TO FIT. Five lazy-loading variants were BUILT and measured
before this number was chosen, not estimated:
ChatView lazy                     -2,903 B
landing sections below Hero lazy  -4,669 B  (whole strip)
AccountMenu lazy                    -865 B
ToastHost lazy                      -390 B
None was taken, and the reasons are about the product, not the bytes:
- ChatView is the target of the primary CTA. Deferring it puts a network
fetch in front of the app's main interaction to buy 4.4%; making that
honest needs a prefetch, which is machinery added purely to serve a
number. It stays eager, deliberately.
- The landing strip IS a real candidate -- deferring below-the-fold
marketing content is defensible on its own merits -- but the measured
-4,669 B variant also moved QuestionTicker and SourcesStrip, which sit
just under the Hero. The defensible shape needs landing-sections.tsx
physically split and an IntersectionObserver mount, with its own
measurement and its own pass over the 22 visual baselines. That is a work
package, not a line in this one. Tracked, with these numbers, in
docs/BACKLOG.md.
- AccountMenu and ToastHost are rejected on merit: one pops in inside the
header, the other would add a round-trip to display the error toast that
fires precisely when the network is already unhappy.
SO WHAT DOES 68,000 MEAN. The graph measures 66,394 B as this lands, leaving
1,606 B (2.4%). Ordinary work in this repo is a few hundred bytes: the four
accessibility fixes in this PR cost +306 B in total (+197 B for the arriving-
answer announcement, +104 B for the restored toast, +5 B for the `/` shortcut
fix), each measured by building with that change alone removed. So the
headroom is about five more changes of this size -- enough that a normal PR is
not a budget event, and small enough that the trend is still visible.
WHAT IT PROTECTS AGAINST, precisely: a STEP CHANGE. A new npm dependency, or a
whole new surface imported eagerly instead of via React.lazy. Those are
kilobytes -- so any of them lands over this line immediately and has to be
argued for. MEASURED TODAY, corrected in place rather than contradicted six
lines later (which this file has done before): the lazy SURFACES are Nudge
1,226 B, HistoryDrawer 1,287 B, ConnectedAccountsDrawer 1,636 B, AuthModal
2,894 B and landing-strip 4,722 B gzip -- so 1.2-4.7 kB, not the 1.2-2.9 kB
this sentence claimed before #358 landed the strip. The three shared helper
chunks are smaller still (79, 495 and 778 B gzip), so that range names
surfaces, not every emitted chunk. It does NOT try to police tens of bytes,
because policing tens of bytes is what produced #355's neighbour and the cut
toast.
AND BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT THIS FILE DOES NOT DO. Nothing goes red if you raise
EITHER number. A reviewer set the eager one to 500,000 and the entire suite
stayed green; the same is true of the lazy one. The validation on both is
`Number.isInteger(max) && max > 0` plus, since #372, a test asserting the
enforced-key SET is exactly these two -- so ADDING or DROPPING a key is now
visible, while EDITING a value still is not. The control is the DIFF, and the
person reading it, not a test. That is the accepted design (a number in a
file beats prose in a docs row, which is what it replaced), but it is a
REVIEW control: do not read a green build as agreement.
WHAT WOULD JUSTIFY RAISING IT AGAIN. Not 'the build got bigger'. Name the
module that grew and its MEASURED bytes (build once with the change removed --
the arithmetic above is the pattern), and say why it must be eager. If the
answer is 'a new screen/modal/panel', it should be a dynamic import instead,
like AuthModal, HistoryDrawer, ConnectedAccountsDrawer, Nudge and
landing-strip already are.
If the answer is 'a new dependency', that is a dependency decision, and the
byte cost belongs in the PR body next to it.
AND WHAT WOULD JUSTIFY LOWERING IT. Landing the landing-strip split above.
Ratchet this number DOWN in the same PR that frees the bytes, or the win is
silently spent by the next three changes.
The landing-strip split described above LANDED, so this number came down in
the same PR that freed the bytes -- which is what the paragraph directly
above demanded of it.
MEASURED, both by `npm run check:bundle` on the shipping variant:
before  66,394 B gzip   (ceiling 68,000, headroom 1,606)
after   62,873 B gzip   (ceiling 64,479, headroom 1,606)
freed    3,521 B
WHY 64,479 AND NOT SOMETHING ROUNDER. It is 62,873 + 1,606: the headroom WAS
SET at EXACTLY what the 68,000 decision chose, so this was a pure ratchet.
Past tense on purpose -- 'is held' was present tense and this PR's own TODAY
row below falsifies it: the floor has since moved to 62,974 B (#356 spent
101 B), so the headroom against 64,479 is 1,505 B today, not 1,606. That is
the headroom being SPENT, which is what it is for; the ratchet is a statement
about the moment it landed, not a standing invariant.
The bytes the split freed are banked; the room for ordinary work is not
touched. Tightening further would re-create the 69 B situation that made a
WCAG fix the thing someone traded away (PR #357), and that is the failure
this file exists to prevent -- so the win goes to the FLOOR, never to the
headroom.
NOTE THE FIGURE THE ISSUE CARRIED. #358's title says -4,669 B. That was the
whole strip INCLUDING QuestionTicker and SourcesStrip, measured against a
65,931 B graph, and it was never the shippable shape. Re-measured here on
the shape that actually shipped: -3,521 B. The 4,669 figure should not be
quoted for this change.
WHAT THIS GATE NOW STOPS SEEING, STATED PLAINLY. The 3,521 B did not
evaporate -- 4,721 B of it moved OUT from under this gate into a lazy chunk.
For a reader whose observer fires on first paint (see the blind spot below,
which is every desktop viewport measured so far) the first-paint total is:
TODAY   62,974 B + 4,722 B (strip)    = 67,696 B   (re-measured at #372)
The #358-era rows are kept, labelled, because the +1,200 B delta is a
statement about that change; the TODAY row is what `npm run check:bundle`
prints now. landing-strip.tsx is byte-identical since #358 and still moved
4,721 -> 4,722 B, because every lazy chunk embeds the entry's content hash
-- so expect +/-1-2 B of perturbation on every lazy chunk whenever eager
code changes, and do not read it as a regression.
So on desktop this change makes first-paint JS BIGGER by 1,200 B, and the win
is one of ORDERING -- a smaller entry chunk that parses and paints sooner,
with the strip arriving on a second non-blocking request. The genuine byte
saving is on phone-sized viewports, where the sentinel starts outside the
lead margin and a reader who does not scroll never fetches those 4,721 B.
That is the trade, made deliberately and on purpose in that direction: bytes
matter most on the metered, slow connections, which are the phones.
Say this out loud whenever the -3,521 B is quoted.
A DATED RECORD OF TWO CLAIMS THIS CHANGE FALSIFIED. BOTH ARE NOW CORRECTED
IN PLACE, ABOVE, where a reader meets them -- this block is the log of what
they used to say, not a live correction, because doing half in place and
half 130 lines later is the exact self-contradiction this file documents and
it was doing it as recently as #372's first round:
- 'lazy SURFACES are 1.2-2.9 kB' (until #358). Corrected in place at WHAT
IT PROTECTS AGAINST: landing-strip is a lazy surface at 4,722 B gzip, so
the range is 1.2-4.7 kB. That matters because the range is the ARGUMENT
for why a new eager surface lands over the line immediately -- it must
describe the surfaces that exist.
- 'react-dom ... 63.6% ... read it as ~64%' (until #372). That share was
of the PRE-CHANGE graph. Against the raw graph that ships -- 192,912 B
when #358 wrote the line, 193,208 B measured today -- the same 130,102 B
is 67.4% / 67.3%. Corrected in place at WHAT THE GRAPH ACTUALLY IS. The
point it was making is unchanged and gets STRONGER: app code shrank, so
React is an even larger share of what is left, and no app-code change
moves the dominant term.
AND THE BLIND SPOT THIS CHANGE WALKS UP TO. The blind-spot list above says
`dynamicImports` is the STATIC/DYNAMIC split, not the eager/lazy one, and
that the two coincide only while every dynamic import sits behind a user
action or a scroll. Until #372 that list said 'as all four of this app's do
today' and named four clicks; #372 corrected it IN PLACE to FIVE, so do not
read the sentence quoted here as the file's current text -- it is the dated
record of what it used to say. The fifth surface, landing-strip, is behind a
SCROLL rather than a click. Measured, not assumed: on
Desktop Chrome 1280x720 the sentinel sits 854 px down, inside the 400 px
lead margin, so that reader's observer fires on first paint and fetches the
chunk anyway -- this gate does not count those 4.7 kB. On a 390x844 phone
the sentinel is at 1458 px and the deferral is real. So the honest claim for
desktop is 'off the critical path', not 'never downloaded' -- and the byte
arithmetic that follows from it is spelled out above under WHAT THIS GATE
NOW STOPS SEEING. Both viewports are pinned in
frontend/tests/lazy-strip.spec.ts, but NOT symmetrically: the phone side is
an ASSERTION (the sentinel must start outside the lead margin, and zero
chunk requests may happen before the scroll), while the desktop side is
RECORDED as a test attachment plus a request count. Asserting the desktop
inequality would go red if a taller Hero made desktop start deferring too --
an improvement -- and a check that fails when the behaviour gets better
locks in the weaker behaviour.
ADDED lazyChunkGzipMaxBytes = 6328 (#372, 2026-09-08)
WHAT #372 ACTUALLY COMPLAINED ABOUT. Not that lazy chunks were unbounded --
that they were unbounded AND the gate REPORTED A WIN. #358 freed 3,521 B from
the eager chunk, `npm run check:bundle` said so, and nothing in that output
said desktop first-paint JS had grown 1,200 B or that all-JS had grown at all.
The fix is therefore TWO things, and only the first is a gate:
1. ONE new ENFORCED key. A PER-CHUNK gzip ceiling on every emitted .js chunk
that is not in the eager closure.
2. RECORDED reporting. `npm run check:bundle` now prints, on EVERY run and on
BOTH the pass and the fail path of both verdicts: the per-chunk lazy
table with each chunk's headroom, the largest lazy chunk, the lazy SUM,
the all-JS TOTAL, and the count of manifest records skipped as non-.js.
WHAT THAT DOES NOT DO, because the first version of this paragraph
overclaimed it and a reviewer was right: those numbers go to a CI LOG.
They are not in the diff, not in a tracked file, and nothing asserts
them, so a PR body quoting an eager-only win is exactly as available as
it was before. What changed is that the countervailing numbers are now
PRODUCED on every run that gets as far as measuring, on both verdict
paths, so a reader who opens the log has them. Closing the rest of the
gap needs the numbers IN THE DIFF -- a recorded-measurements file this
gate rewrites and a reviewer sees change -- which is a separate work
package, not this one.
WHY 6328. It is 4,722 (landing-strip, today's largest lazy chunk, measured) +
1,606, the headroom the 68,000 decision chose and the 64,479 ratchet preserved
at the moment it landed -- so the lazy ceiling was DERIVED from the same
constant rather than from a second number nobody can reconstruct. Note the two
keys' headrooms have since diverged and that is normal, not a defect: the lazy
headroom is still 1,606 B (the strip has not moved), while the eager headroom
is 1,505 B (64,479 - 62,974) because #356 spent 101 B of it. A headroom
constant is what a ceiling is SET from; it is not a standing invariant, and
the earlier claim that this file 'keeps ONE headroom constant' was present
tense and false. Re-derive 6,328 the same way if the largest lazy chunk
changes.
HOW THE LAZY SET IS COMPUTED, and why the obvious way is WRONG. It is a SET
DIFFERENCE: every emitted .js `file` in the manifest, minus
`eagerChunkFilesFromManifest`. It is NOT a walk out from `dynamicImports`
following `imports`. In this app's REAL manifest the three `_`-prefixed shared
chunks each declare an `imports` array whose ONLY entry is `index.html` -- a
BACK-EDGE pointing at the ENTRY -- so a walk reaches the entry, files the
62,974 B entry chunk as 'lazy', and it clears the 6,328 B ceiling only by being
mis-classified. A fixture modelling that back-edge is in
scripts/bundle-budget.test.mjs; it is the test a traversal-based
reimplementation fails.
WHAT WAS REJECTED, AND WHY (this is load-bearing; do not re-litigate)
The issue proposed TWO keys. Both were falsified.
REJECTED: a TOTAL-JS ceiling. Three reasons that hold, and a fourth that was
listed FIRST and called the strongest until a reviewer checked its
arithmetic. Read the order as fixed, not as an invitation to re-rank:
1. IT WOULD HAVE HAD TO BE RAISED BY THE PR THAT RATCHETED THE EAGER KEY
DOWN -- which the WHAT WOULD JUSTIFY LOWERING IT paragraph above demanded
of that same PR. Two keys pulling opposite ways in one diff is not a
budget, it is a negotiation with itself.
2. ITS ADVERTISED VIRTUE IS SYMMETRIC. If eager -> lazy is byte-neutral to a
total, so is lazy -> eager. Folding all five lazy surfaces back into the
entry LOWERS the total (five import prologues and the three shared chunks
disappear) while first-paint JS goes 62,974 -> ~76,000 B. A total key does
not punish the exact step change the eager key exists to catch.
3. IT IS NOT AN UPPER BOUND ON FIRST-PAINT BYTES ANYWAY. It over-reports
first-paint JS by 8,395 B on desktop and 13,117 B on phone, and excludes
9,169 B of render-blocking CSS, the two self-hosted fonts, and everything
in frontend/public/.
4. DEMOTED, AND SAY WHY. This read 'IT WOULD HAVE GONE RED FOR #358' and was
the first and strongest reason listed. It does not follow. Reconstructed
from this file's own recorded figures, all-JS before #358 was ~74,789 B
and after ~75,989 B, +1,200 B. But a ceiling in this repo is never set AT
the measurement: it is set at measurement + headroom, which is what the
68,000, the 64,479 and the 6,328 decisions above all did. Apply this
file's own convention -- 74,789 + 1,606 = 76,395 -- and #358 lands at
75,989 with 406 B to spare: GREEN. The claim is true only for a
ZERO-HEADROOM total ceiling, a condition the sentence never stated and
this file's practice contradicts. What survives is weaker and worth
keeping: a total key's verdict on #358 depends ENTIRELY on an arbitrary
headroom constant, where the eager key's verdict does not. That is a
reason to distrust a total key, not a demonstration that it fires wrong.
(The 8,395 B 'other lazy' term in that arithmetic is MEASURED AT HEAD,
not at #358, so both reconstructed figures carry that approximation.)
The DECISION stands on reasons 1-3, which were reproduced independently and
hold. So the total is RECORDED on every run instead. A number a reader sees is
worth more than a ceiling whose verdict is set by the constant you pick.
REJECTED: a FIRST-PAINT ceiling (`firstPaintGzipMaxBytes`). The issue named its
own input: 'lazy-strip.spec.ts already records the desktop request count; that
is the input'. It cannot be. VERIFIED by reading frontend/playwright.config.ts:
`webServer.command` is `npm run dev` and the env sets VITE_API_LIVE to the
string false, so that suite runs against the Vite DEV server, which serves
unbundled ES modules. There are no production chunks and no gzip sizes there to
read. Any first-paint key would also be VIEWPORT-DEPENDENT, and see C1 below.
WHAT THE NEW KEY CATCHES, AND WHAT IT STILL CANNOT
CATCHES: a lazy chunk crossing a line without anyone editing this file. Before
#372 a lazy surface could grow to any size at all and no command said anything.
CANNOT: the line being EDITED. Raising either number still turns nothing red --
see the paragraph above. The one thing that changed is that ADDING or DROPPING
an enforced key is now visible: src/test/buildGuards.test.ts pins both key
NAMES as literals and asserts the enforced-key SET is exactly those two.
C1, stated so it is not undone by accident: the new key is VIEWPORT-BLIND on
purpose, and frontend/tests/lazy-strip.spec.ts's desktop/phone asymmetry stays
as it is. No check here may go red when desktop STARTS deferring.
BLIND SPOTS OF THE NEW KEY, in the style of the list above and measured, not
asserted:
- CSS: 9,169 B gzip. Bounded by neither key.
- The SUM of the lazy chunks: 13,117 B. Bounded by nothing, RECORDED only.
- The COUNT of the lazy chunks: 8. A PER-CHUNK ceiling actively REWARDS
splitting one chunk into two, which costs one more round trip, and nothing
here counts round trips. This is a real evasion, not a theoretical one --
frontend/tests/lazy-strip.spec.ts:130 already names the two-boundaries,
one-module shape that exists to avoid it.
- The UNCONDITIONAL module-scope `import()` described in the blind-spot list
above, which this key SANCTIONS at 6,328 B rather than merely missing.
- frontend/public/: about-theme.js is 1,512 B raw and is not in the manifest
at all. The demonstrated 73,869 B render-blocking script-src path stays
closed only because src/test/buildGuards.test.ts pins the single `<script>`
in index.html.
- The two self-hosted fonts.
- The DESKTOP FIRST-PAINT TOTAL, 62,974 + 4,722 = 67,696 B today. No key
bounds it, deliberately: asserting it would go red the day a taller Hero
makes desktop START deferring -- an improvement -- and a check that fails
when the behaviour gets better locks in the weaker behaviour. That is the
same reason lazy-strip.spec.ts records the desktop geometry instead of
asserting it.
- +/-1-2 B of perturbation on EVERY lazy chunk whenever eager code changes,
because each lazy chunk embeds the entry's content hash. Measured:
landing-strip.tsx is byte-identical since #358 and still went 4,721 ->
- THE CEILING IS SLACK FOR SEVEN OF THE EIGHT CHUNKS. It was derived from
the LARGEST one, so it binds that one and almost nothing else. Measured,
as ceiling / chunk: landing-strip 1.34x, AuthModal 2.19x,
ConnectedAccountsDrawer 3.87x, HistoryDrawer 4.92x, Nudge 5.16x,
ProviderIcons 8.13x, useFocusTrap 12.8x, the shared index chunk 80.1x. So
seven of the eight can MORE THAN DOUBLE before this key says a word --
AuthModal could add 3,434 B and Nudge 5,102 B in silence. A per-chunk
ceiling set from the maximum is a step-change detector for one chunk and
a very loose one for the rest; that is the accepted trade (the
alternative is eight numbers to maintain), not an unnoticed gap.
- A BRAND-NEW LAZY SURFACE MAY BE BORN AT 6,327 B and this gate stays
silent -- 1.34x the largest chunk that exists today, arriving with no
history to compare against. The key catches GROWTH past a line; it does
not ask whether a new surface should have been that size to begin with.
That is a review question, and this file cannot answer it.
